WarningSigns.title: A new lump, thickening, or dimpling
WarningSigns.sign_name: Palpable lump, skin dimpling, or breast tissue change
WarningSigns.description: A new lump you can feel — most often in the upper outer quadrant. Or dimpling of the skin (like an orange peel). Or an area where the skin puckers, thickens, or the breast changes shape. Anything that wasn’t there last month and is there now.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: Any of these can be an early sign of breast cancer. Lumps that are hard, immovable, and painless are the classic red flag — but plenty of cancers present as soft, movable, or tender lumps too. Skin dimpling and puckering are underrated because they don’t feel like anything. You have to look.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: Most breast lumps are benign — cysts, fibroadenomas, or hormonal thickening tied to your cycle. The odds are in your favor. But "probably benign" is not a diagnosis. Only imaging is a diagnosis.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
Here is what will likely happen if you’re under 40: your doctor will feel the lump, tell you it’s "fibrocystic changes," and suggest you come back in a few months if it’s still there. This is not a rule-out. This is a guess wearing a lab coat.

You are entitled to imaging. Ask for it directly: "I want an ultrasound to rule out anything concerning. If it looks suspicious, I want a diagnostic mammogram." Do not accept "wait and watch" as a first response when you can feel something that wasn’t there before.

If you’re over 40 and this is a screening year, you’re due for a mammogram regardless. A new lump moves you into diagnostic imaging. Different billing code, different urgency, same-week appointment.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• A new lump that lasts through a full menstrual cycle (or 4+ weeks if post-menopausal)
  • Any skin dimpling, puckering, or orange-peel texture
  • Nipple retraction (a nipple that suddenly turns inward)
  • Any change in breast size, shape, or symmetry that’s new
  • Persistent unexplained breast pain in one specific spot
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Rapid onset of breast redness, warmth, and swelling — this can be inflammatory breast cancer, which is aggressive and time-sensitive (mimics mastitis, gets misdiagnosed constantly)
  • A breast lump with high fever, spreading redness, and severe pain
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: Ask specifically: "Can you order an ultrasound? If not, I’d like a referral to a breast specialist." If your PCP won’t refer you, you can self-refer to most breast imaging centers with a script or through a direct patient program. You do not need permission to get imaging for a lump you can feel.
WarningSigns.family_history_note: If a first-degree relative had breast cancer before age 50, or if there’s a family history of ovarian, pancreatic, or male breast cancer — you may qualify for BRCA testing and earlier/annual MRI screening. Ask for genetic counseling.

WarningSigns.title: Nipple discharge that isn’t breastmilk
WarningSigns.sign_name: Spontaneous nipple discharge, especially bloody or clear
WarningSigns.description: Fluid coming from one or both nipples without you squeezing it out. Especially concerning if it’s spontaneous (stains your bra), bloody, or clear-and-watery — and if it’s from one duct in one breast.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: Bloody or clear nipple discharge from a single duct is the classic sign of an intraductal papilloma (usually benign) or ductal carcinoma in situ (early breast cancer). Any spontaneous discharge in a non-lactating breast needs imaging, full stop.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: Milky discharge from both breasts is usually hormonal — often prolactin-related (pituitary, medications like SSRIs, or thyroid). Not cancer. But that’s a specific pattern, and it should still be worked up.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
Nipple discharge is one of the more embarrassing things to bring to a doctor, and doctors know it. Which is why so many will nod politely and say "let’s see if it stops on its own." No.

The workup for nipple discharge is not optional. It should include: a clinical exam, an ultrasound, a mammogram (if you’re over 30), and sometimes an MRI or ductogram. If you get discharge and a shrug, you did not get evaluated.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Any nipple discharge that’s bloody, clear, or one-sided
  • Discharge that happens without you touching the breast
  • Discharge from a single duct (one dot, not multiple)
  • Discharge combined with a lump, skin change, or nipple retraction
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er: • Discharge with high fever, spreading redness, and severe breast pain (possible abscess)
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: Say the words: "I need this worked up with imaging. What’s the plan?" If they refer to it as "probably nothing" — that’s the moment to ask for a referral to a breast surgeon or breast center. Not because you need surgery — because those clinics take single-duct discharge seriously.

WarningSigns.title: Rectal bleeding under 50
WarningSigns.sign_name: Blood in stool, on toilet paper, or in the toilet bowl
WarningSigns.description: Visible blood — bright red on the paper, streaked through stool, or in the bowl. Also counts: dark, tarry, sticky stools (this suggests bleeding higher up in the digestive tract). Also counts: iron-deficiency anemia showing up on bloodwork without an obvious cause.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: Colorectal cancer rates in adults under 50 have nearly doubled since the 1990s. Rectal bleeding is one of the earliest and most-dismissed signs. If you’re under the recommended screening age (45 per current USPSTF guidance), your doctor is statistically likely to write this off as hemorrhoids without ruling anything out.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: Most rectal bleeding is hemorrhoids, anal fissures, or diet-related irritation. That is genuinely true. But "probably" is not "definitely," and only a scope tells you the difference.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
If you’re under 45 with rectal bleeding, you WILL be told it’s hemorrhoids. This is not a fluke — it is the default. "You’re young" gets treated as a diagnosis when it isn’t one.

Younger colorectal cancer patients wait an average of 6 months longer for diagnosis than older patients. Not because the science is harder. Because their symptoms are dismissed on sight. You do not need to be polite about this.

The exact ask: "I want this ruled out with a physical exam and a colonoscopy referral if warranted. Not next year. Now." If your doctor won’t refer, get a second opinion or request a GI consult directly.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Any rectal bleeding lasting more than a few days
  • Any change in bowel habits (constipation, diarrhea, thin stools) lasting 3+ weeks
  • Unexplained weight loss (more than 5% of body weight without trying)
  • Persistent abdominal cramping, gas, or the feeling that your bowel doesn’t empty completely
  • New iron-deficiency anemia on bloodwork without a clear cause (heavy periods excepted)
  • Extreme fatigue that isn’t explained by sleep or life
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Heavy bleeding (soaking through pads, filling the bowl, or with clots)
  • Dizziness or lightheadedness with the bleeding
  • Dark tarry stools with fatigue or lightheadedness (signals significant blood loss)
  • Severe abdominal pain, especially with fever or vomiting
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: Ask directly: "Can you rule this out with a rectal exam and, if needed, a colonoscopy referral?" You are allowed to insist. If they refuse, request the refusal in writing — this almost always changes the answer. You can also self-refer to most GI practices with a doctor’s note, or through direct-access screening programs like ColonoscopyAssist.com.
WarningSigns.family_history_note: If a first-degree relative had colorectal cancer, your screening age drops to 10 years before their diagnosis, or age 40 — whichever comes first. Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis push it earlier still. Push for a colonoscopy referral even if you’re under 45. This is your birthright, not a favor.

WarningSigns.title: Sudden change in bowel habits
WarningSigns.sign_name: New constipation, diarrhea, thin stools, or incomplete emptying
WarningSigns.description: Your bowels changed and stayed changed. New constipation (fewer than 3 movements a week when you used to have daily). New diarrhea lasting weeks. Stools that come out pencil-thin. The feeling that you never fully empty. Alternating between constipation and diarrhea without a dietary reason.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: Persistent bowel changes lasting more than 3 weeks can signal a partial obstruction from a colorectal tumor. Thin stools especially — think of the tumor as narrowing the passage. Not all cancers cause thin stools, but the pattern is worth naming.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: IBS, food sensitivities, medication changes (opioids constipate, antibiotics loosen), stress, or GI infections. These are far more common. But cancer hides among common things, which is why "just IBS" needs to be earned by workup, not assumed.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
IBS is real, but it’s also the medical dumping ground for anything a doctor doesn’t want to work up. If you got an "IBS" diagnosis without a colonoscopy, stool testing, or celiac panel — you got a shrug in a diagnosis costume.

A proper workup for persistent bowel changes should include: stool tests for blood and inflammation markers (fecal immunochemical test, calprotectin), a celiac panel, and — if you’re over 45 or symptomatic — a colonoscopy. Anything less is triage, not diagnosis.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Bowel changes that persist beyond 3 weeks without a clear cause
  • New thin/pencil-shaped stools
  • Persistent feeling of incomplete evacuation
  • Bowel changes with unexplained weight loss or fatigue
  • Bowel changes with rectal bleeding
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Complete inability to pass stool or gas for more than 24 hours with abdominal distension (possible obstruction)
  • Severe abdominal pain with vomiting
  • Bloody diarrhea with fever
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: If you’re told "it’s just IBS" without stool testing or (if appropriate) a scope, that’s not a diagnosis. Ask: "What have we ruled out? Can we do a FIT test and a calprotectin?" Both are cheap, non-invasive, and specifically screen for the things a shrug misses.

WarningSigns.title: The ABCDE of a suspicious mole
WarningSigns.sign_name: A mole that is asymmetric, has an irregular border, uneven color, is large, or is evolving
WarningSigns.description: The five features that separate a benign mole from one that needs a biopsy: Asymmetry (one half doesn’t match the other). Border irregularity (jagged, notched, or blurred edges). Color variation (multiple browns, black, red, white, or blue). Diameter over 6mm (about the size of a pencil eraser). Evolution — any mole that’s changing.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: Melanoma is the most dangerous skin cancer, but it’s also one of the most curable when caught early. A mole that meets 2+ ABCDE criteria is a candidate for biopsy. Evolution is the most important — a mole that’s changing is a mole that needs eyes on it, no matter how "normal" it looks.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: Most moles are benign. Dysplastic (atypical) moles are common and mostly harmless. But melanomas often start looking like ordinary moles, which is why "watchful waiting" without dermoscopy is a bet, not a plan.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
The words "it looks fine" from a rushed PCP glance are not a skin exam. A real skin check uses dermoscopy (a lit magnifier), takes measurements, and photographs anything suspicious for comparison next year.

If your primary care doctor eyeballed a mole for 5 seconds and said "looks fine," you did not get a skin check. You got a courtesy peek. Ask for a referral to dermatology, or find a dermatology clinic that offers annual full-body skin exams (many charge under $200 without insurance).
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Any mole that’s changing in size, color, shape, or symptoms
  • A new mole appearing after age 30
  • A mole that itches, bleeds, or scabs without healing
  • A mole that’s visibly different from your others (the "ugly duckling")
  • Any dark spot under a fingernail or toenail (subungual melanoma is often missed)
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er: • Skin cancers are not ER situations — but a rapidly growing, bleeding, ulcerated lesion warrants same-week dermatology, not next-month scheduling
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: Ask directly: "Can you use a dermatoscope and photograph this for comparison?" If they can’t, request a dermatology referral. If your insurance requires a referral and your PCP won’t give one, dermatology practices often accept self-referrals for a fee. That’s worth it.
WarningSigns.family_history_note: A first-degree relative with melanoma triples your risk. Multiple family members with melanoma, pancreatic cancer, or eye melanoma may signal familial atypical multiple mole syndrome (FAMMM). Ask about annual (not periodic) dermatology screening.

WarningSigns.title: A sore that won’t heal
WarningSigns.sign_name: A wound, lesion, or ulcer that persists beyond 4 weeks
WarningSigns.description: A sore, scab, or ulcer that keeps showing up in the same spot. On the skin (especially sun-exposed areas — face, ears, scalp, forearms, hands). In the mouth. On the genitals. It might bleed, scab over, seem to heal, then come back. Or it might just stay open.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: Non-healing sores are how basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas often show up on skin. In the mouth, a non-healing ulcer can signal oral cancer. On the genitals, HPV-related cancers. These are not exotic diagnoses — they’re common cancers with clear early signs that get ignored because "it’s just a sore."
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: Most non-healing skin sores are caused by scratching, friction, chronic sun damage, or infection. Mouth sores are usually canker sores or bites. Genital sores are usually irritation or herpes. Cancer is not the first bet — but 4+ weeks is the line where "probably" needs to be verified.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
A doctor telling you "just keep it moisturized" or "just rinse with salt water" is not treating your sore. They’re hoping it goes away so they don’t have to think about it.

The rule is simple: any sore that hasn’t healed in 4 weeks needs a biopsy. Not a bigger tube of ointment. A biopsy. This is a 10-minute procedure, mostly billed as a preventive dermatology visit.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Any skin sore lasting more than 4 weeks
  • Any oral ulcer lasting more than 2 weeks
  • Any genital sore lasting more than 3 weeks
  • Sores that bleed, ooze, or scab repeatedly in the same spot
  • A sore combined with numbness, tingling, or hardening of surrounding tissue
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Rapidly enlarging, bleeding, infected sore with fever
  • Sudden severe pain or spreading redness (cellulitis)
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: The one-line ask: "This has been here more than 4 weeks. I want a biopsy." Most dermatologists will do it same-visit. PCPs often can too, and if they can’t, they’ll refer. For oral sores, ask a dentist as well as an MD — dentists catch a lot of early oral cancers because they’re looking.

WarningSigns.title: A cough that won’t quit
WarningSigns.sign_name: Persistent cough lasting 3+ weeks, especially with any of these features
WarningSigns.description: A cough that hangs on past 3 weeks. It might be dry or productive. It might be worse at night, worse with exercise, or constant. It might have started with a cold that never fully left. Especially concerning if you’re coughing up blood, if your voice has changed, or if you’re short of breath doing things that used to be easy.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: A persistent cough is the most common early sign of lung cancer. It’s also the sign most likely to get labeled "post-viral," "seasonal," or "just a smoker’s cough" and left alone. Lung cancer is diagnosed at Stage IV in over half of cases because early signs get normalized.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: Post-viral cough (can linger 8 weeks after a cold or flu). Asthma. Post-nasal drip. GERD. Bronchitis. Vaping-related airway irritation. These are the actual likely causes. But lung cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women and the leading cause of cancer death — and 15-20% of lung cancer diagnoses are in never-smokers.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
You do not have to be a smoker to get lung cancer. This is one of the most stubborn medical myths, and it costs lives. Rates of lung cancer in never-smokers — especially women — are rising, and no one is sure why. The Mayo Clinic and NCI have both flagged this trend.

If your doctor treats "never smoked" as a rule-out, that’s outdated. Ask directly: "Given this cough won’t quit, can we get a low-dose chest CT?" You may be told you don’t qualify for the screening version (which is age-and-smoking gated). That’s fine — a diagnostic chest CT for a persistent cough is different and is medically justified.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Cough lasting more than 3 weeks
  • Coughing up blood, even a streak (hemoptysis)
  • Voice change or hoarseness lasting more than 2 weeks
  • Shortness of breath doing things that used to be easy
  • Chest, shoulder, or upper back pain with the cough
  • Recurrent chest infections (2+ in a year)
  • Unexplained weight loss or fatigue with the cough
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Coughing up large amounts of blood
  • Severe shortness of breath at rest
  • Chest pain with sweating, nausea, or arm/jaw pain (rule out heart)
  • Blue lips or fingernails
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: If you’re told "it’s just post-viral" or "try inhalers first," give it a defined window — 2-4 more weeks. If it doesn’t resolve, come back and ask: "What’s the plan to rule out anything structural? Can we get a chest CT?" A regular chest X-ray misses a lot of early lung cancers; a CT catches them.

WarningSigns.title: Chest pain that changes with breathing
WarningSigns.sign_name: Chest, shoulder, or upper back pain that’s worse with deep breaths, coughs, or laughs
WarningSigns.description: A specific kind of chest pain — the kind that gets worse when you take a deep breath, cough, or laugh. It might feel like a stitch, a stab, or a dull ache that ramps up with lung expansion. It might radiate to the shoulder or upper back. It might be constant or come in waves.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: Pain that changes with breathing (pleuritic pain) suggests the lung lining is involved — which happens with pleural effusion, pulmonary embolism, pleurisy, or a tumor pressing on the chest wall. Lung cancers that grow near the pleura or ribs often present this way, and they’re easy to miss because "chest pain" gets triaged for heart, not lung.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: Muscle strain, costochondritis (rib inflammation), a lingering viral pleurisy, or a rib injury you don’t remember. These are the actual likely causes. But pleuritic pain deserves a chest workup, not just an ibuprofen script.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
Chest pain that isn’t "classic heart attack" gets deprioritized. Especially in women, who are less likely to be worked up for cardiac causes AND less likely to be worked up for pulmonary causes. The result: "it’s probably muscular" as a diagnosis by default.

If pleuritic chest pain is new, persistent, and paired with any of the lung red flags above (cough, shortness of breath, weight loss), ask for a chest CT. Not an X-ray. A CT. X-rays miss a lot of the things you’re trying to rule out.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Chest pain that consistently gets worse with deep breathing
  • Chest pain lasting more than a few days without a clear cause
  • Chest pain with cough, shortness of breath, or fever
  • Chest pain paired with unexplained weight loss or fatigue
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Sudden, severe, or crushing chest pain
  • Chest pain with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or arm/jaw pain
  • Chest pain with coughing up blood
  • Chest pain with rapid heart rate or lightheadedness (rule out pulmonary embolism)
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: If your workup was "listened to your lungs and pressed on your chest," you got a physical exam, not a diagnosis. Ask: "Can we get imaging — chest CT if X-ray is normal?" Especially if the pain has lasted more than 2 weeks and other lung symptoms are present.

WarningSigns.title: Urinary changes over 50
WarningSigns.sign_name: Weak stream, frequent nighttime urination, hesitancy, or incomplete emptying
WarningSigns.description: Getting up more than once or twice a night to pee. A urinary stream that starts and stops or feels weaker than it used to. Hesitancy — you’re at the urinal but nothing’s happening. The feeling of not fully emptying. Sometimes pain or burning. Sometimes blood.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: These are the classic signs of prostate enlargement — and yes, they overlap almost exactly with the signs of prostate cancer. That overlap is why prostate cancer is often "found" during routine BPH workup, and also why it’s missed when the workup is skipped.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) — the prostate enlarges with age and squeezes the urethra. This is the most likely cause for most men over 50. Urinary tract infections and bladder issues are next. But the workup to distinguish BPH from cancer is routine bloodwork, not surgery.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
The PSA test has a controversial history. It was over-recommended in the 2000s, leading to over-treatment of slow-growing prostate cancers. In response, USPSTF pulled back their recommendation, and many PCPs stopped ordering PSAs at all. The pendulum swung too far. Prostate cancer deaths are ticking back up in some populations, and the reason is likely that shared-decision-making has become "your doctor doesn’t bring it up."

If you’re over 50 (or over 45 if Black or with family history) and having urinary symptoms, you have the right to a PSA test and a digital rectal exam. Ask for both. Interpret the PSA in context with your urologist, not off a single number. But get the test.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Urinary symptoms lasting more than a few weeks
  • Blood in urine or semen (any amount)
  • Painful ejaculation
  • Erectile dysfunction that’s new or worsening
  • Persistent pain in the pelvis, hips, or lower back (advanced sign — don’t wait)
  • Any of the above in a Black man over 45, or any man with a father/brother history of prostate cancer
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Complete inability to urinate (acute urinary retention)
  • Fever with urinary symptoms (possible prostate infection or urosepsis)
  • Severe hematuria (blood in urine) with pain
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: The exact ask: "I’d like a PSA test and a digital rectal exam. I understand the tradeoffs and I want the baseline." If your doctor pushes back on PSA testing, ask them to document their reasoning. That documentation almost never gets written down, and asking for it often changes the response.
WarningSigns.family_history_note: Black men have a 60% higher risk of prostate cancer and are more than twice as likely to die from it. If you’re Black, screening should start at 45, and if there’s family history, at 40. If a father or brother had prostate cancer — especially before 65 — start at 40. These earlier screening ages are supported by the American Urological Association and the American Cancer Society.

WarningSigns.title: Blood in urine or semen
WarningSigns.sign_name: Visible blood in urine (hematuria) or semen (hematospermia)
WarningSigns.description: Pink, red, or tea-colored urine. Blood streaks or spots in semen. Sometimes visible only in the toilet bowl. Sometimes only picked up on a urine dipstick as "microscopic hematuria" on routine labs.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: Blood in urine can be a sign of prostate cancer, bladder cancer, kidney cancer, or a urinary tract cancer higher up. Bladder cancer in particular is often missed because "one episode of blood" gets attributed to a UTI without follow-up. Microscopic hematuria — the kind picked up on lab tests — has cancer as a cause in roughly 5% of cases, which is high enough to always work up.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: UTIs (especially in women). Kidney stones. Prostate enlargement. Recent vigorous exercise. Menstrual contamination. Certain medications and foods (beets, some dyes). These are far more common than cancer. But hematuria of any kind that isn’t clearly explained needs imaging.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
If you had one episode of bloody urine, got treated for a UTI, and never had a follow-up urine test to confirm the blood was gone — you got half a workup. The rule: hematuria that doesn’t clear with treatment needs imaging and cystoscopy.

For microscopic hematuria on lab tests: the current guideline is CT urogram plus cystoscopy for anyone over 35 with any risk factor (smoking, chemical exposure, family history, or the blood persisting). Most PCPs will say "recheck in 6 months." That’s not the guideline. That’s their comfort level.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Any visible blood in urine, even one episode
  • Any blood in semen (especially over 40, or persistent)
  • Microscopic hematuria on any routine urinalysis
  • Painful urination with blood
  • Flank (side) pain with blood in urine
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Heavy bleeding with clots in urine
  • Blood in urine with high fever (possible pyelonephritis/urosepsis)
  • Blood in urine with severe flank pain
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: Ask for imaging directly: "Can we get a CT urogram to rule out an upper tract source? And a urology referral for cystoscopy if the blood persists?" Both of those are standard workup for hematuria over 35. Anything less is a shortcut.

WarningSigns.title: Bleeding between periods or after sex
WarningSigns.sign_name: Intermenstrual bleeding, postcoital bleeding, or postmenopausal bleeding
WarningSigns.description: Bleeding when you shouldn’t be. Between periods. After sex. After menopause. Spotting that comes and goes. Especially concerning if it’s heavy, if there’s pain, or if there’s an unusual discharge with it.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: Cervical cancer often shows up as bleeding after sex or between periods — because the cervix is fragile and cancerous tissue bleeds on contact. Postmenopausal bleeding (any bleeding at all after 12 months of no periods) is a classic sign of endometrial cancer and requires workup — no exceptions.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: Hormonal fluctuations. Missed pills. Ovulation spotting. Fibroids. Polyps. Cervical irritation. Perimenopausal changes. All far more common than cancer. But cervical and endometrial cancers hide in this exact symptom pattern, so "probably hormones" needs to be earned by workup.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
This is one of the most consistently dismissed cancer symptoms in medicine. Women get told they’re "in perimenopause" or "on the wrong pill" or "stressed" for months, sometimes years, before someone orders an ultrasound.

The workup for abnormal bleeding is not optional and it is not slow: a pelvic exam, a Pap smear + HPV test (if not current), a transvaginal ultrasound, and if you’re over 45 or postmenopausal — an endometrial biopsy. Anything less is triage, not diagnosis.

For postmenopausal bleeding specifically: any bleeding, any amount, needs a biopsy. There is no acceptable "let’s watch it." The risk of endometrial cancer in postmenopausal bleeding is around 10%, which is nowhere near "wait and see" territory.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Any bleeding after sex
  • Bleeding between periods that persists more than 2-3 cycles
  • Any bleeding at all more than 12 months after your last period
  • Bleeding with pelvic pain, unusual discharge, or a foul odor
  • Heavier periods than usual, especially if you’re over 40
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Very heavy bleeding (soaking a pad an hour for several hours)
  • Bleeding with severe pelvic pain, fainting, or dizziness
  • Bleeding with fever and pelvic pain (possible infection)
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: Say the words: "This bleeding is abnormal and I want it worked up with imaging and, if warranted, a biopsy." If your provider offers a birth control adjustment as the first move without imaging, that’s an acceptable first pass ONLY if you’re under 40, low-risk, and it resolves within 1-2 cycles. If you’re older or if it doesn’t resolve — insist on the workup.

WarningSigns.title: Unusual vaginal discharge
WarningSigns.sign_name: Watery, bloody, or foul-smelling discharge that’s new or persistent
WarningSigns.description: Discharge that’s different from your normal — watery, blood-tinged, or with a smell you can’t attribute to infection. Especially concerning when it’s persistent (weeks, not days), heavy, and doesn’t respond to typical treatments for yeast or bacterial vaginosis.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: Cervical and vaginal cancers can cause chronic watery or bloody discharge. Advanced cervical cancer sometimes causes a foul-smelling discharge from tissue breakdown. These are late-ish signs, but they’re unmistakable once you know what you’re looking at.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: Yeast infections. Bacterial vaginosis. STIs. Cervicitis. Atrophic changes after menopause. Retained foreign objects (tampons). All far more common than cancer. But the "we tried three creams and it’s still here" pattern is where it stops being routine.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
The pattern here is: try yeast cream → try antibiotics → try boric acid → try another antibiotic. Somewhere in that loop, someone should have said "let’s look at the tissue." Often, no one does.

If you’ve had persistent unusual discharge for more than a few weeks and empirical treatments haven’t worked, ask for a pelvic exam with visualization, a Pap smear, an HPV test, and (if appropriate) a colposcopy. A colposcopy is a magnified look at the cervix and takes 10 minutes.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Discharge that’s different from your baseline and persists more than 2 weeks
  • Blood-tinged discharge outside your period
  • Discharge with a foul or unusual odor that persists after treatment
  • Discharge with pelvic pain, itching that won’t resolve, or visible lumps/lesions
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Discharge with high fever and severe pelvic pain (possible pelvic inflammatory disease or infection)
  • Discharge with heavy vaginal bleeding
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: The ask: "When was my last Pap and HPV test? Are they up to date? I want a pelvic exam and visualization. If nothing obvious shows, I want a colposcopy." HPV testing is more sensitive than Pap alone for cervical cancer screening, and combining them (co-testing) is the current standard for women 30-65.
WarningSigns.family_history_note: HPV is the primary cause of cervical cancer, and vaccination status matters more than family history here. If you were vaccinated for HPV, your risk is significantly lower — but not zero. If you weren’t (many women over 40 weren’t offered it), your Pap+HPV testing schedule matters even more.

WarningSigns.title: Persistent bloating that won’t quit
WarningSigns.sign_name: Bloating, feeling full quickly, or pelvic pressure lasting 2+ weeks
WarningSigns.description: Bloating that doesn’t resolve with the usual fixes. Feeling full after a few bites (early satiety). Pelvic pressure or discomfort. Sometimes a visibly distended abdomen. What sets this apart from normal cyclical bloating: it doesn’t come and go with your period. It stays.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: Ovarian cancer is called "the silent killer" for a reason — it barely produces symptoms until late stages, and the symptoms it does produce (bloating, fullness, pelvic pressure) look exactly like a hundred other benign things. Persistent bloating is one of the earliest signs, and one of the most gaslit.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: IBS. Food intolerance. Hormonal shifts. Perimenopause. Stress. Constipation. These are almost always the actual cause. Ovarian cancer is rare — but its symptoms are common, which is exactly why doctors miss it.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
Ovarian cancer patients see an average of 3 doctors before someone takes them seriously. The average delay from first symptom to diagnosis is 6-9 months. Not because the science is hard — because "bloating in a woman over 40" is treated as normal by default.

If your doctor tells you "it’s probably just hormones" or "just perimenopause" or "try eliminating gluten" without ordering a pelvic exam, transvaginal ultrasound, and CA-125 blood test, they haven’t ruled anything out. They’ve made a guess.

The exact ask: "I want a pelvic exam, a transvaginal ultrasound, and a CA-125 to rule out ovarian cancer. When can we do them?" If they push back, ask why in writing. That question changes the answer roughly 80% of the time.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Bloating lasting 2+ weeks straight, or 12+ days per month for 2+ months
  • Feeling full quickly, or unable to finish normal meal portions
  • New pelvic pressure, discomfort, or a feeling of heaviness
  • Urinary urgency or frequency without infection
  • Changes in bowel habits alongside bloating
  • Unexplained weight loss or gain
  • Abnormal bleeding paired with any of the above
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Severe or sudden abdominal pain
  • Inability to keep food or fluids down
  • Sudden visible distension with fever
  • Distension with severe pain, especially if you had ovarian cysts (possible torsion)
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: Ask for a referral to a gynecologic oncologist or, at minimum, a gynecologist who specializes in pelvic imaging. If your PCP won’t refer, request the refusal in writing. That paperwork alone almost always unblocks the referral. Alternatively, self-refer to a gyn practice — most will see you.
WarningSigns.family_history_note: BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations dramatically raise ovarian cancer risk. If you have any family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, or prostate cancer — especially early-onset — request genetic counseling. Lynch syndrome also raises risk. Some women with high-risk mutations opt for prophylactic salpingo-oophorectomy; that’s a real conversation to have with a specialist.

WarningSigns.title: Feeling full quickly (early satiety)
WarningSigns.sign_name: Unable to finish normal meal portions; a few bites feel like a full meal
WarningSigns.description: You sit down to eat a meal you’d normally finish. A few bites in, you feel full. Sometimes uncomfortably so. Sometimes with mild nausea. This isn’t "I’m watching my portions" — it’s "my body is telling me it’s done and it wasn’t like this six months ago."
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: Early satiety is one of the classic "vague but specific" cancer symptoms. It shows up in ovarian, pancreatic, and gastric cancer — all of which are hard to detect early because their symptoms mimic ordinary GI complaints. When early satiety persists for more than a few weeks without a clear cause, it moves out of "probably nothing" and into "worth working up."
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: Gastritis. GERD. Gastroparesis (delayed stomach emptying, common with diabetes). Anxiety-related eating changes. Medication side effects. Ordinary aging changes in metabolism. These are the actual likely causes. But the workup is quick and worth doing.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
Early satiety often gets waved away as "eating less as you get older" or "your metabolism slowing down" or "probably reflux." No workup, no imaging, no follow-up.

A proper workup for persistent early satiety includes: a physical exam, basic bloodwork, a pelvic ultrasound (in women), and — if there’s any weight loss or other symptoms — a CT of the abdomen and pelvis. Anything less is not a workup.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Early satiety lasting more than 3-4 weeks without a clear cause
  • Combined with unintended weight loss
  • Combined with bloating, pelvic pressure, or abdominal discomfort
  • Combined with new-onset nausea or vomiting
  • Combined with jaundice, changes in stool color, or upper abdominal pain (concerning for pancreatic or gastric causes)
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Inability to keep any food or fluids down
  • Severe abdominal pain with early satiety
  • Bloody vomit or coffee-ground vomit
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: Ask: "Can we get a pelvic ultrasound and, if that’s normal, a CT of the abdomen and pelvis? Given how long this has lasted, I want to rule out anything structural." That specific framing usually unlocks the imaging.

WarningSigns.title: New-onset diabetes after 50
WarningSigns.sign_name: Diabetes diagnosed after age 50 without typical risk factors, or diabetes that’s suddenly hard to control
WarningSigns.description: You’re over 50. You’re not overweight, or you haven’t had significant weight gain. You don’t have a strong family history of diabetes. But your blood sugar is climbing and you’ve been told you have type 2 diabetes. Or: you’ve had well-controlled diabetes for years, and suddenly it’s not controlled anymore, even though nothing’s changed.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: New-onset diabetes in adults over 50 is associated with a 6-8x increased risk of pancreatic cancer being diagnosed within 3 years. This is one of the most-cited early signs of pancreatic cancer, and one of the most under-recognized by primary care. The mechanism: pancreatic tumors can disrupt insulin production, causing what looks like type 2 diabetes but is actually a paraneoplastic effect.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: Actual type 2 diabetes. Age-related insulin resistance. Steroid-induced hyperglycemia. Weight gain. Family history you didn’t know about. These are far more common. But the pancreatic cancer link is real enough that current research is exploring whether new-onset diabetes over 50 should trigger pancreatic screening.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
You will almost certainly not be told about the pancreatic connection when you’re diagnosed with adult-onset diabetes. Your PCP will hand you metformin, some lifestyle advice, and a follow-up. That’s the standard of care, and for the vast majority of people it’s correct.

But if you’re over 50, have no strong diabetes risk factors, and especially if you’ve lost weight or had unexplained abdominal or back pain, ask directly: "Should we consider pancreatic imaging given my age and profile?" The current research (see the NOD initiative — New-Onset Diabetes) is building toward this as a screening trigger. You can ask for it now.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• New diabetes diagnosis over 50, especially without excess weight
  • Sudden loss of diabetes control after years of stability
  • Diabetes onset combined with unintended weight loss
  • Diabetes with new-onset abdominal or upper back pain
  • Diabetes with jaundice, dark urine, or pale stools
  • Diabetes with new or worsening depression (paraneoplastic depression is a known pancreatic cancer sign)
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Diabetic ketoacidosis symptoms (severe thirst, fruity breath, confusion, vomiting)
  • Severe abdominal pain radiating to the back
  • Sudden jaundice with pain
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: The ask: "Given my age and lack of typical risk factors, can we consider pancreatic imaging? Or at least establish a baseline lipase and CA 19-9?" These aren’t definitive tests, but they’re a starting point. A CT of the abdomen with pancreatic protocol is the gold standard when clinical suspicion is meaningful.
WarningSigns.family_history_note: A family history of pancreatic, breast, ovarian, or melanoma cancer can signal BRCA-related risk (yes, BRCA affects pancreatic cancer too). Lynch syndrome, hereditary pancreatitis, and familial atypical multiple mole syndrome all raise pancreatic risk. If two or more relatives on the same side had these cancers, ask about genetic counseling and possibly annual MRI screening.

WarningSigns.title: Painless jaundice
WarningSigns.sign_name: Yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes without abdominal pain
WarningSigns.description: Your skin, or the whites of your eyes, look yellowish. Sometimes you notice it in the mirror; more often, someone else notices first. Your urine may be dark. Your stools may be pale, clay-colored, or floating. And — critically — you don’t have severe abdominal pain to explain it.
WarningSigns.what_it_could_mean: Painless jaundice is one of the most specific early signs of pancreatic cancer (specifically, tumors at the head of the pancreas that press on the bile duct). It’s also a sign of bile duct cancer and some liver cancers. Any painless jaundice is a same-week workup, not a routine appointment.
WarningSigns.what_it_probably_is: Gallstones (but usually with pain). Hepatitis. Medication-induced liver injury. Gilbert’s syndrome (a benign inherited condition). These are the actual possibilities. But "painless" and "sudden" together shift the differential toward serious quickly.
WarningSigns.commonly_dismissed_note:
Jaundice from anything is a red flag. Painless jaundice is a five-alarm red flag. The workup happens the same week — imaging (CT or MRCP), liver enzymes, bilirubin fractionation, tumor markers.

If you notice yellowing and are told "come back in a month" — that is not an acceptable timeline. Ask for imaging this week. If your PCP can’t make that happen, go to urgent care or the ER. This is one of the few situations where "wait and see" can cost you a stage.
WarningSigns.when_to_call_doctor:
• Any yellowing of the skin or eyes
  • Persistently dark urine (tea-colored, without dehydration)
  • Pale or clay-colored stools
  • Jaundice with unintended weight loss
  • Jaundice with itching (bile acid buildup causes intense whole-body itch)
  • Jaundice paired with new diabetes, back pain, or fatigue
WarningSigns.when_to_go_to_er:
• Painless jaundice of any kind (yes, this is ER-appropriate — do not wait for routine scheduling)
  • Jaundice with fever or severe pain (possible cholangitis)
  • Sudden confusion or mental status change with jaundice (possible hepatic encephalopathy)
WarningSigns.if_dismissed: This is not a symptom to be diplomatic about. The words: "This is painless jaundice. I need same-week imaging — CT abdomen or MRCP — and a GI or hepatology consult." If you get scheduled more than a week out, go to urgent care with the same request. This is one place where escalation is not optional.

AccessGuides.title: Get your mammogram fully covered (yes, really)
AccessGuides.overview: Under the Affordable Care Act, screening mammograms are covered at 100% — no copay, no coinsurance, no deductible — for women 40 and older (and earlier if high-risk). Most people don’t know this. Clinics don’t always volunteer it. Insurers routinely miscode the visit. But if you know the exact word to use when booking, you never pay a dime.
AccessGuides.steps:
The magic word is screening. When you call to schedule, say "I’d like to book a screening mammogram" — not "a mammogram," not "a diagnostic mammogram," not "a follow-up." The billing code for a screening mammogram (CPT 77067) is 100% covered by ACA-compliant insurance. The billing code for a diagnostic mammogram (CPT 77065 or 77066) is not — it goes toward your deductible.

Same machine. Same technician. Same 15 minutes. Different code, different bill.

When they check you in at the clinic, verify one more time: "This is being coded as a screening mammogram, correct?" If you have a lump, symptoms, or a callback — that’s diagnostic, and you may pay. If it’s your routine annual — it should be screening, and you should not.
AccessGuides.when_applies:
• You have ACA-compliant insurance (most plans since 2014)
  • You’re 40+ and getting a routine annual mammogram
  • You’re under 40 but qualify as high-risk (family history, BRCA, prior chest radiation)
  • You have Medicare (screening mammograms are covered annually with no cost-sharing)
AccessGuides.when_not:
• You have symptoms (lump, discharge, pain) — that’s diagnostic
  • You’re on a "grandfathered" pre-ACA plan (rare now, but check)
  • You need supplemental screening (ultrasound, MRI) — coverage varies (see dense breast guide)
  • You need callback imaging after an abnormal screening — that’s diagnostic (but new 2022 federal rules require some plans to still cover it)
AccessGuides.resources:
National Breast and Cervical Cancer Early Detection Program (NBCCEDP): Free or low-cost mammograms for women who qualify by income. Find your state’s program at cdc.gov/cancer/nbccedp or call 1-800-232-4636.

Susan G. Komen Screening Assistance: Local affiliates offer screening funds. Call the Komen Helpline at 1-877-465-6636 or visit komen.org.

American Cancer Society Road to Recovery: Free rides to screening and treatment appointments. 1-800-227-2345.
AccessGuides.denial_path: ACA-compliant plans cannot legally charge you for a screening mammogram (CPT 77067). If you’re billed anything, this is a coding error roughly 90% of the time. Call your insurer, cite ACA Section 2713 preventive care coverage, and ask them to reprocess the claim. Get the reference number. If they refuse, file a written appeal — most states require insurers to respond within 30 days. If that fails, file a complaint with your state insurance commissioner (contact info at naic.org).

AccessGuides.title: Get your colonoscopy fully covered
AccessGuides.overview: Screening colonoscopies for adults 45-75 are covered at 100% under the ACA — no copay, no coinsurance, no deductible. This includes the polypectomy (polyp removal) if one is found during the same procedure. That last part matters, because it used to be a huge billing loophole where a "screening" colonoscopy turned into "diagnostic" the moment they removed a polyp, and patients got surprise bills. That loophole was closed in 2022.
AccessGuides.steps:
Confirm three things when scheduling: (1) you’re booking a screening colonoscopy, (2) you’re within the covered age range (45-75, or earlier with risk factors), (3) the facility and anesthesia providers are in-network. The colonoscopy itself is 100% covered, but anesthesia and pathology can be out-of-network at an in-network facility — this is the classic surprise bill. Ask specifically: "Are the anesthesiologist and the pathology lab in my network?"

If a polyp is found and removed during your screening colonoscopy, this is still covered as screening under current federal rules. If you get billed for the polypectomy separately — that’s a coding error and you appeal it.
AccessGuides.when_applies:
• You have ACA-compliant insurance
  • You’re 45-75 and this is your routine screening (10-year interval)
  • You’re under 45 but have family history or genetic risk (start earlier)
  • You have Medicare (screening colonoscopy covered every 10 years, or every 24 months if high-risk)
AccessGuides.when_not:
• You have symptoms (bleeding, bowel changes) — that’s diagnostic
  • You’re getting a follow-up colonoscopy after a positive stool test (this SHOULD be covered under 2022 rules, but plans sometimes misapply — appeal if billed)
  • You’re getting a shorter-interval colonoscopy because of previous polyps — this may be diagnostic depending on plan
AccessGuides.resources:
ColonoscopyAssist (colonoscopyassist.com): Reduced-cost colonoscopies for people without insurance ($1,075-$1,595 depending on region — a fraction of retail price).

Colorectal Cancer Alliance Blue Star Program: Financial assistance and coordination for people who qualify. 1-877-422-2030 or ccalliance.org.

FIT (fecal immunochemical test) as a screening alternative: Under $30 retail, covered as screening under ACA. Not a replacement for colonoscopy long-term, but a valid annual screening.

Cologuard (stool DNA test): Covered under ACA for average-risk adults 45+, once every 3 years. Not for high-risk patients. Positive result requires follow-up colonoscopy.
AccessGuides.denial_path: If you get a bill for a screening colonoscopy — even after a polyp removal — call your insurer and cite the 2022 federal rule (Section 2713 clarification, effective 2022) that requires follow-up services during a screening colonoscopy to be covered at 100%. Get the claim reprocessed. If they refuse, appeal in writing. If that fails, complaint to state insurance commissioner.

AccessGuides.title: Get a skin check without insurance
AccessGuides.overview: Skin cancer screening is one of the easiest cancer screenings to get without insurance. Full-body skin exams from a dermatologist typically cost $100-$250 out of pocket. Free screening events happen year-round through the American Academy of Dermatology. And self-checks — when done right — catch most concerning changes before a professional does.
AccessGuides.steps:
Three tiers of access, cheapest first: (1) AAD SPOTme free screenings — free full-body skin exams by volunteer dermatologists, listed at aad.org/public/public-health/skin-cancer/skin-cancer-screening. Events are seasonal but frequent. (2) Direct-pay dermatology visits — most derm practices offer cash-pay skin checks in the $100-$250 range. Call and ask for the "self-pay skin exam" price. (3) Teledermatology services — for a single suspicious spot, apps like MDLIVE, SkinIO, and Dermatology On Call offer $50-$80 asynchronous consults. Not a substitute for a full-body exam, but good for triage.

For self-checks: do one every month. Use a mirror or a partner for hard-to-see areas (back, scalp, buttocks). Photograph anything that looks unusual, use the ABCDE criteria (asymmetry, border, color, diameter, evolution), and compare against last month’s photos. Self-checks catch roughly half of melanomas before they’re diagnosed by a doctor.
AccessGuides.when_applies:
• You don’t have insurance
  • Your insurance doesn’t cover dermatology, or requires a referral you can’t get
  • You have insurance but want to skip the referral and just self-pay
  • You have a single spot you’re worried about (teledermatology is fast and cheap)
AccessGuides.resources:
American Academy of Dermatology SPOTme program: Free skin cancer screenings held nationwide. aad.org/public/public-health/skin-cancer/skin-cancer-screening.

The Skin Cancer Foundation: Directory of free screening events plus education resources. skincancer.org.

Impact Melanoma Practice Safe Skin: Free skin cancer screenings and education, especially in schools and workplaces. impactmelanoma.org.

Community health centers (HRSA-funded): Offer dermatology services on a sliding-scale basis. Find yours at findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov.
AccessGuides.denial_path: If your insurance denies a skin check as "not medically necessary," the workaround is to have a specific concern documented — a mole that’s changing, a family history of melanoma, a new lesion. That reframes the visit as diagnostic and typically triggers coverage. If you’re at high risk (fair skin, history of sunburns, family melanoma), some insurers cover annual skin exams as preventive; ask explicitly.

AccessGuides.title: Get a Pap smear and HPV test at zero cost
AccessGuides.overview: Cervical cancer screening — Pap smear, HPV test, or both together (co-testing) — is covered at 100% under the ACA for women 21-65. This is one of the most successful cancer screenings in history: cervical cancer deaths have dropped by more than half since routine Pap testing became standard. And it’s essentially free if you know how to book it.
AccessGuides.steps:
Book it as a well-woman visit or preventive care visit — not as a "problem visit." That distinction is what triggers 100% coverage under ACA Section 2713. If you have specific symptoms, mention them, but the visit code should still be preventive first.

Current guidance from ACS: Pap every 3 years for women 21-29. Pap + HPV co-test every 5 years for women 30-65 (or HPV test alone every 5 years). Beyond age 65, screening usually stops if you’ve had consistent normal results. This is different from USPSTF, which recommends Pap every 3 years for 21-29 and Pap or HPV or co-test every 3-5 years for 30-65. Both are within the ACA-covered range.

If you’ve had HPV vaccination (Gardasil), you still need screening — the vaccine covers most but not all cancer-causing HPV strains.
AccessGuides.when_applies:
• You have ACA-compliant insurance
  • You’re 21-65 (some plans cover through 65 or beyond with risk factors)
  • You have Medicare (Pap smears covered every 24 months, annually if high-risk)
  • You have Medicaid (varies by state, but usually covered)
AccessGuides.resources:
National Breast and Cervical Cancer Early Detection Program (NBCCEDP): Free or low-cost Pap and HPV testing for women who qualify by income. cdc.gov/cancer/nbccedp.

Planned Parenthood: Sliding-scale Pap smears and HPV tests, often at rates far below other clinics. Call 1-800-230-7526.

Community health centers (HRSA): Sliding-scale rates. findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov.

Local health departments: Often provide free or low-cost screening, especially during Cervical Cancer Awareness Month (January) and Women’s Health Week (May).
AccessGuides.denial_path: If you’re billed for a preventive Pap smear or HPV test, it’s a coding error. Call the insurer, cite ACA preventive coverage, and request reprocessing. The most common error: the visit was coded as "problem-focused" when it should have been "preventive." Ask your provider’s billing office to fix the code and resubmit.

AccessGuides.title: Low-dose CT lung screening — who qualifies free
AccessGuides.overview: Low-dose CT (LDCT) is the only lung cancer screening tool proven to reduce mortality. It’s covered at 100% under ACA and Medicare for people who meet the specific USPSTF criteria. That criteria matters — because if you fall within it, this is free, and if you don’t, it might be a hard sell to your insurance.
AccessGuides.steps:
The USPSTF 2021 criteria for free annual LDCT: age 50-80, 20+ pack-year smoking history, current smoker or quit within the last 15 years. A pack-year is one pack a day for one year (or two packs a day for six months — same thing). If you fit all three criteria, this is a covered preventive service. Book it as "lung cancer screening" and confirm coverage in advance.

If you don’t meet criteria — because you’ve been quit longer, because you were a lighter smoker, or because you never smoked — LDCT can still be ordered by your doctor if there’s clinical justification (persistent cough, family history, exposure history). It won’t be free, but retail price is typically $200-$400. And a diagnostic chest CT for a specific symptom is a different pathway that’s often covered.

Never-smokers with concerning symptoms (cough, weight loss, hemoptysis): a chest CT ordered as diagnostic (not screening) is your route. The screening pathway is not for you, but the diagnostic pathway is available and appropriate.
AccessGuides.when_applies:
• You’re 50-80, have 20+ pack-years of smoking, and currently smoke or quit within 15 years
  • You have ACA-compliant insurance or Medicare
  • You get screened annually (once per year, following abnormal findings protocol if applicable)
AccessGuides.when_not:
• You don’t meet the age/smoking criteria (may still get diagnostic imaging with symptoms)
  • You quit smoking more than 15 years ago
  • You’ve never smoked (unless there’s a specific occupational or clinical trigger)
AccessGuides.resources:
American Lung Association Lung Cancer Screening Initiative: Directory of accredited screening centers plus financial assistance info. Lung.org or 1-800-586-4872.

Free to Breathe (a program of LUNGevity): Financial assistance for lung cancer patients (not screening, but valuable if diagnosed). lungevity.org.

Community LDCT programs: Some hospital systems offer $99 self-pay LDCT for people who don’t qualify. Ask locally.
AccessGuides.denial_path: If you meet all USPSTF criteria and are denied — that’s incorrect application of ACA rules. Cite Section 2713 and the USPSTF Grade B recommendation for lung cancer screening. If you’re denied for not meeting criteria, work with your doctor to document the clinical justification for a diagnostic chest CT instead — different pathway, but often covered when symptoms warrant.

AccessGuides.title: PSA testing when your doctor won’t order it
AccessGuides.overview: PSA testing for prostate cancer screening is in a strange place. USPSTF gives it a Grade C recommendation for men 55-69 (meaning "shared decision-making"), and doesn’t recommend it at all for men 70+ (Grade D). Because of the Grade C status, many PCPs no longer proactively offer PSA testing. If you want one and your doctor won’t order it, you have real options.
AccessGuides.steps:
First: ask directly and specifically. "I’d like to have a PSA test as part of my screening. I understand the tradeoffs and I want the baseline." That framing (informed decision, not passive request) usually unlocks the order. Most PCPs will order it if you specifically ask — the issue is they don’t offer.

Second: if your doctor still refuses, you can order a direct-to-consumer PSA test. Companies like Everlywell, LetsGetChecked, and Quest Direct offer PSA tests for $50-$100 without a doctor’s order. Results come with reference ranges, and you can bring them to your doctor for interpretation.

The result to know: PSA under 4 ng/mL is generally normal for men over 50, but the trend over time (velocity) matters more than any single number. A rising PSA is more meaningful than a "high" one-time reading. Ask for annual testing to establish a trend.
AccessGuides.when_applies:
• You’re a man 40+ wanting a baseline PSA (screening starts at 40 if Black or family history; otherwise 50)
  • You have symptoms that warrant workup (urinary changes, blood in urine or semen)
  • You want ongoing monitoring after a previous PSA result
AccessGuides.resources:
ZERO Prostate Cancer: Free PSA screening events nationwide, plus financial assistance for testing and treatment. zerocancer.org or 1-888-244-9137.

Us TOO Prostate Cancer: Support and screening advocacy. ustoo.org.

The Prostate Cancer Foundation: Research funding + patient support resources. pcf.org.

Direct-to-consumer PSA testing: Everlywell ($59), LetsGetChecked ($89), Quest Direct ($69). No doctor order required.
AccessGuides.denial_path: PSA testing is generally covered by ACA-compliant plans for men 50+ when ordered by a physician. If your PCP won’t order it and you use direct-to-consumer, that’s out of pocket. If your PCP orders it and insurance denies, cite USPSTF Grade C shared-decision-making guidance and ACA preventive care rules for men 55-69. Most denials get reversed on appeal.

AccessGuides.title: Appealing a denied diagnostic mammogram
AccessGuides.overview: A diagnostic mammogram (one done because of symptoms, callback, or dense breasts) is not automatically covered at 100% under ACA. But as of 2022, updated federal rules require most plans to cover follow-up imaging after an abnormal screening mammogram at no cost. And many states (17+ as of 2026) have passed laws requiring 100% coverage of diagnostic mammograms full stop. If you’re billed for one, the appeal path is well-worn.
AccessGuides.steps:
Step 1: Find out if your state requires coverage. As of 2026, states with laws requiring 100% coverage of diagnostic mammograms include Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, New Hampshire, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Rhode Island, Texas, Virginia, Washington, and West Virginia. Check current list at densebreast-info.org.

Step 2: Cite the correct rule when you call. For follow-ups after an abnormal screening: cite the 2022 federal rule clarifying that supplementary services related to screening must be covered without cost-sharing. For any diagnostic mammogram in a state with a coverage law: cite that specific state law.

Step 3: File a written appeal. Include: the date of service, the CPT code (usually 77066 for diagnostic), the reason it was diagnostic (symptoms, callback, dense breasts, etc.), and the specific federal or state rule that requires coverage. Insurers must respond within 30 days.

Step 4: If denied on appeal, file a complaint with your state insurance commissioner. Contact info at naic.org. This step often unlocks the coverage — insurers hate state regulator involvement.
AccessGuides.resources:
Susan G. Komen Financial Assistance: For diagnostic imaging and treatment costs. komen.org or 1-877-465-6636.

CancerCare Copayment Assistance: cancercare.org or 1-800-813-4673.

DenseBreast-info.org: Comprehensive state-by-state coverage law tracker plus advocacy resources.
AccessGuides.denial_path: Written appeals go to the insurer’s appeals department (address on your denial letter). Include documentation of the diagnostic necessity from your provider. If your first appeal is denied, request an external review — the insurer must provide one, and external reviewers overturn denials roughly 40% of the time.

AccessGuides.title: HSA and FSA money you didn’t know you could use
AccessGuides.overview: HSA (Health Savings Account) and FSA (Flexible Spending Account) money is pre-tax dollars you can spend on qualifying medical expenses. Most people use them for copays and glasses. But the eligible expense list is much bigger than that, and it includes a surprising amount of cancer prevention and detection.
AccessGuides.steps:
What you can use HSA/FSA for that most people don’t know: genetic testing (BRCA panels via Color, Invitae, etc. — often $200-$500 self-pay), skin cancer teledermatology consults, direct-to-consumer PSA and colon screening tests (Cologuard, ColoHealth), copays for diagnostic imaging that isn’t fully covered, SPF sunscreen (yes, it counts if it’s primarily SPF), self-monitoring devices (breast exam trainers, glucose monitors), and travel costs to specialists (mileage, parking, sometimes lodging).

HSA vs FSA: HSA rolls over year to year and is yours to keep. FSA is use-it-or-lose-it, sometimes with a small carryover ($640 in 2026). If you have both options, the "use FSA first at end of year, save HSA for later" strategy makes sense.

The 2026 contribution limits: HSA up to $4,300 individual / $8,550 family (add $1,000 catch-up if 55+). FSA up to $3,300 per year.
AccessGuides.when_applies:
• You have an HSA or FSA through work
  • You have HSA-eligible high-deductible health insurance (allowing you to open an HSA)
  • You have expenses that qualify (see IRS Publication 502 for the full list)
AccessGuides.resources:
IRS Publication 502 (medical expense guide): irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p502.pdf. This is the source of truth for what qualifies.

HSAstore.com and FSAstore.com: Retail sites that only sell HSA/FSA-eligible products. Useful for confirming eligibility.

Fidelity HSA, Lively, HealthEquity: HSA providers that offer investment options once you have a base balance (usually $1,000+). HSA money can be invested and grown tax-free.
AccessGuides.denial_path: HSA/FSA claims are usually reimbursed by your plan administrator, not your insurance company. If a claim is denied, appeal with documentation showing the expense qualifies under IRS rules (a letter of medical necessity from your doctor helps for anything borderline). Most administrators approve on appeal when documentation is provided.

AccessGuides.title: No-insurance cancer screening — the real list
AccessGuides.overview: If you don’t have insurance, you can still get every major cancer screening. The list of free and low-cost programs is longer than most people realize, but scattered across dozens of organizations, and access varies by state, income, and cancer type. Here’s the practical map.
AccessGuides.steps:
Start with two searches: (1) Your state’s NBCCEDP program (National Breast and Cervical Cancer Early Detection Program) — cdc.gov/cancer/nbccedp. (2) Your nearest HRSA-funded community health center — findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov. Between these two, you can typically access breast, cervical, and colon screening for free or on a sliding scale, plus general primary care.

For colon: ColonoscopyAssist.com offers colonoscopies for $1,075-$1,595 nationally (still a lot, but 60-70% below retail). FIT tests are under $30 and mail-in. Cologuard costs $700-$800 without insurance but is often covered by state Medicaid.

For skin: American Academy of Dermatology SPOTme free screenings (aad.org). Impact Melanoma. Community derm practices offering self-pay ($100-$250).

For prostate: ZERO Prostate Cancer free screening events (zerocancer.org). Direct-to-consumer PSA tests ($59-$89).

For lung: Some hospital systems offer $99 low-dose CT for people who don’t qualify for ACA-covered screening. Call your local imaging center.
AccessGuides.resources:
NBCCEDP (breast + cervical): cdc.gov/cancer/nbccedp — free/low-cost for women who qualify by income (usually under 250% of federal poverty).

HRSA Community Health Centers: findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov — sliding-scale primary care and screening, no insurance required.

Planned Parenthood: 1-800-230-7526 — sliding-scale for cervical, breast, and general reproductive care.

ColonoscopyAssist: colonoscopyassist.com — reduced-cost colonoscopies for uninsured.

ZERO Prostate Cancer: zerocancer.org — free PSA screening events.

AAD SPOTme (skin): aad.org — free dermatology screening events.

American Cancer Society: 1-800-227-2345 — general information and referrals to local resources.

RxAssist and NeedyMeds: rxassist.org and needymeds.org — patient assistance for medications and screening tests.
AccessGuides.denial_path: These are direct-access programs, not insurance-based, so there’s no denial to appeal. If you’re turned down for income reasons, ask about sliding-scale options or ask the intake worker if there’s another program that fits your income tier.

AccessGuides.title: Genetic testing (BRCA, Lynch) — when it’s covered
AccessGuides.overview: Genetic testing for cancer risk — BRCA1/BRCA2 (breast, ovarian, prostate, pancreatic risk), Lynch syndrome (colon, endometrial, other), and multi-gene panels — is one of the most powerful preventive tools in medicine. Testing is often 100% covered when you meet specific family history criteria. But if you don’t meet those criteria, testing is affordable out of pocket ($150-$300), and knowing your status can change your screening schedule for life.
AccessGuides.steps:
The covered pathway: you’re covered if you meet NCCN or USPSTF criteria. For BRCA: a personal or family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, or prostate cancer, especially at younger ages, or Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry with any relevant family history. For Lynch: a personal or family history of colon or endometrial cancer, especially early-onset (before 50), or a family member with a known mutation. Full criteria at nccn.org.

The self-pay pathway: Color Health, Invitae, and MyGeneCounsel offer clinician-ordered panels for $250-$500. 23andMe offers a limited BRCA test for a subset of mutations for around $200 (Ashkenazi variants only — this is important; a "negative" 23andMe result does NOT rule out BRCA if you’re not Ashkenazi).

Genetic counseling should ideally happen BEFORE testing, not after — a counselor helps you decide which panel is right for you and what to do with the results. Most testing companies include free virtual counseling. If you’re going through insurance, most policies require pre-test counseling.
AccessGuides.when_applies:
• You have a personal history of cancer (especially breast, ovarian, colon, endometrial, pancreatic)
  • You have a family history of these cancers, especially in first-degree relatives, especially before age 50
  • You have Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry (1 in 40 carry a BRCA mutation vs. 1 in 400 in the general population)
  • You have a family member with a known BRCA, Lynch, or related mutation
  • You have a specific type of cancer where testing changes treatment (triple-negative breast, ovarian, metastatic prostate, pancreatic)
AccessGuides.resources:
National Society of Genetic Counselors: nsgc.org — find a genetic counselor.

Color Health: color.com — clinician-ordered BRCA + Lynch panels from $250.

Invitae: invitae.com — comprehensive multi-gene cancer panels, sometimes covered via research programs.

Basser Center for BRCA: basser.org — advocacy, research, and community for BRCA carriers.

FORCE (Facing Our Risk of Cancer Empowered): facingourrisk.org — support and advocacy for hereditary cancer risk.
AccessGuides.denial_path: If testing is denied for "not meeting criteria," get a genetic counselor to write a letter of medical necessity referencing NCCN guidelines. Most denials are reversed. If not, self-pay is affordable and the information is yours forever.

AccessGuides.title: Getting a second opinion without your first doctor knowing
AccessGuides.overview: You are legally entitled to a second opinion, and you don’t need permission from your first doctor to get one. Insurance covers second opinions in almost all circumstances (some plans even require them for major surgeries or cancer treatment decisions). The tricky part isn’t the right — it’s the mechanics of getting your records, scheduling, and not making things awkward with your original team.
AccessGuides.steps:
Step 1: Request your records without saying why. Federal law (HIPAA) requires providers to release your records within 30 days of a written request. Ask for: (a) all imaging with the actual images, not just reports (request DICOM discs), (b) pathology slides (not just reports — actual slides that can be re-read at another institution), (c) all clinic notes and test results. You’re allowed to request this without stating a reason.

Step 2: Book the second opinion at a different health system. Major cancer centers (MD Anderson, Memorial Sloan Kettering, Mayo Clinic, Dana-Farber, Johns Hopkins, Cleveland Clinic) all have second opinion programs. Many offer remote/telehealth second opinions where you upload your records and get a written review — no travel required.

Step 3: Verify insurance coverage in advance. Most plans cover second opinions when requested through in-network providers. If the second opinion doctor is out-of-network, some plans will still cover it — call and ask specifically about "second opinion coverage."

You do not need to tell your original doctor unless and until you want to change course based on the second opinion. Records requests are routine and don’t automatically flag "this patient is shopping around."
AccessGuides.when_applies:
• You’ve been given a cancer diagnosis and want confirmation
  • You’ve been given a treatment plan and want to explore alternatives
  • Your doctor has ruled out something you’re worried about, and you want independent verification
  • You’re considering major surgery or aggressive treatment
  • You feel dismissed and want another perspective
AccessGuides.resources:
MD Anderson Second Opinion: mdanderson.org (remote and in-person options).

Memorial Sloan Kettering Second Opinion: mskcc.org.

Mayo Clinic Online Second Opinions: mayoclinic.org.

Cleveland Clinic MyConsult: clevelandclinic.org/online-second-opinion.

Dana-Farber Cancer Institute: dana-farber.org.

The Grayzone Cancer Second Opinion Network: for underinsured patients seeking second opinions on complex cases.
AccessGuides.denial_path: Rare, but if a second opinion is denied by insurance, appeal with a letter explaining the clinical rationale (surgery being considered, treatment decision pending, diagnostic uncertainty). Denials for legitimate second opinion requests are almost always overturned.

AccessGuides.title: Dense breasts — do you qualify for free supplemental imaging?
AccessGuides.overview: About 40% of women over 40 have dense breast tissue, which is common — but it also raises breast cancer risk AND makes mammograms harder to read. Dense tissue looks white on a mammogram, and so does cancer. Supplemental imaging (ultrasound, MRI, contrast-enhanced mammography) catches cancers that mammograms miss in dense breasts. As of 2024, all women in the US receive notification of their breast density after a mammogram. And in more than 30 states, supplemental imaging for dense breasts is covered at no cost.
AccessGuides.steps:
Step 1: Know your density. As of March 2024, federal rules require all mammogram facilities to notify women of their breast density. If you’ve had a mammogram since then, your notification is in your patient portal or your last mammogram report. Categories: A (almost entirely fatty — low density), B (scattered), C (heterogeneously dense), D (extremely dense). C and D count as "dense" for coverage purposes.

Step 2: Check your state’s law. States with laws requiring insurance coverage of supplemental imaging for dense breasts as of 2026 include (partial list) Connecticut, Illinois, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Texas, and more than 25 others. Full current list: densebreast-info.org/legislation.

Step 3: Ask your provider to order supplemental imaging. Options include: whole-breast ultrasound (most commonly ordered, covered in most states with dense breast laws), breast MRI (higher sensitivity but more expensive, usually reserved for high-risk women), contrast-enhanced mammography (newer, growing coverage).
AccessGuides.when_applies:
• You have category C or D breast density (heterogeneously or extremely dense)
  • You live in a state with a supplemental imaging coverage law
  • You have ACA-compliant insurance
  • You have additional risk factors that push you into high-risk category (which qualifies you for MRI in most plans regardless of state law)
AccessGuides.resources:
DenseBreast-info.org: The comprehensive resource on breast density, state laws, and screening recommendations.

AreYouDense.org: Advocacy organization founded by a woman whose invasive cancer was missed on multiple mammograms due to dense breasts.

Susan G. Komen State Advocacy: komen.org/what-we-do/public-policy.

National Breast Cancer Foundation: nationalbreastcancer.org.
AccessGuides.denial_path: If you’re in a state with a supplemental imaging law and denied coverage, cite that specific state statute in your appeal. Include your breast density notification and your provider’s order. If you’re not in a state with a law but meet high-risk criteria (family history, prior chest radiation, personal history, BRCA), request coverage under high-risk screening rules — most plans cover MRI for women with 20%+ lifetime breast cancer risk (via IBIS or Tyrer-Cuzick risk calculators).

AccessGuides.title: When the ACA rule is your best friend (Section 2713)
AccessGuides.overview: Section 2713 of the Affordable Care Act is the single most useful legal foundation for cancer screening access. It requires all ACA-compliant plans to cover — at 100%, with no cost-sharing — every preventive service rated Grade A or B by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF). That covers most cancer screenings across the lifespan. Knowing the exact language of the rule turns most denials into administrative errors.
AccessGuides.steps:
Memorize this sentence for phone calls: "Under ACA Section 2713, my plan is required to cover USPSTF Grade A and B preventive services without cost-sharing. This is a covered service — please reprocess the claim." That specific language, cited by claim number, resolves the vast majority of "I got charged for a screening" issues.

What’s Grade A/B for cancer screening as of 2026: mammogram (biennial, women 40-74); colonoscopy or equivalent (adults 45-75); Pap smear/HPV testing (women 21-65); low-dose CT lung screening (specific age/smoking criteria); PSA (Grade C — shared decision-making, may or may not be covered without cost-sharing depending on plan interpretation); skin cancer screening (Grade I — insufficient evidence, not automatically covered but often covered as part of preventive dermatology).

What’s NOT covered under Section 2713: diagnostic imaging (that’s not preventive), most cancer treatment (that’s not preventive), genetic testing UNLESS you meet criteria (see genetic testing guide), and supplemental imaging (mostly state-law territory).
AccessGuides.when_applies:
• You have any ACA-compliant health insurance (most plans since 2014)
  • You’re getting a service rated USPSTF Grade A or B
  • The service is being coded as preventive/screening (not diagnostic)
AccessGuides.when_not:
• You have a "grandfathered" pre-ACA plan (rare, but possible — check plan documents)
  • The service is diagnostic (has symptoms triggering it, or is a follow-up to abnormal results)
  • The service is Grade C, D, or I (Grade C is shared decision-making; D means not recommended; I means insufficient evidence)
AccessGuides.resources:
USPSTF recommendations: uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org — search any service to check its grade.

HealthCare.gov preventive services list: healthcare.gov/coverage/preventive-care-benefits — the official list of ACA-covered preventive services.

Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS): cms.gov — for Medicare-specific preventive coverage questions.

National Association of Insurance Commissioners: naic.org — state insurance commissioner directory for filing complaints.
AccessGuides.denial_path: If you’re billed for what should be a covered preventive service: (1) call the insurer and cite Section 2713 with the specific USPSTF service grade; (2) if unresolved, file a written appeal; (3) if still denied, request an external review; (4) if still denied, file a complaint with your state insurance commissioner. This ladder resolves the vast majority of screening billing errors.

Therapies.title: Cold caps and scalp cooling — keeping your hair through chemo
Therapies.intro: You may not have to lose your hair. Scalp cooling — either automated cold cap systems (like DigniCap or Paxman) or manual cold caps (like Penguin Cold Caps or Arctic Cold Caps) — can save 50% or more of your hair during many chemo regimens. This is real, FDA-cleared, and criminally under-mentioned b
Therapies.body:
The bottom line

You may not have to lose your hair. Scalp cooling — either automated cold cap systems (like DigniCap or Paxman) or manual cold caps (like Penguin Cold Caps or Arctic Cold Caps) — can save 50% or more of your hair during many chemo regimens. This is real, FDA-cleared, and criminally under-mentioned by oncologists who are busy thinking about your survival, not your ponytail. Both matter.

How it works

Cooling your scalp constricts blood vessels and slows cell metabolism in the follicles, so less chemo drug reaches them. You wear the cap before, during, and after each infusion. Automated systems circulate coolant through a cap connected to a machine at the infusion center. Manual caps are swapped out every 20-30 minutes from a cooler of dry ice — labor-intensive, but portable and often cheaper.

What nobody tells you

Here is the thing your infusion center may not volunteer: scalp cooling has to be arranged in advance. Automated systems need to be available at your center (ask BEFORE your first infusion). Manual caps you rent yourself and bring in — which means you need someone to help you swap them every 20 minutes during a 4-hour infusion. Line this up early.

Success depends on your specific chemo drugs, dose, and hair type. It works best with taxanes, less well with anthracyclines (the "red devil," doxorubicin). Ask your oncologist which drugs you’re getting and how scalp cooling performs with them.
